⟪ἀγαπάω⟫, -ῶ,
[in LXX chiefly for ⁨אהב⁩;] ⟪to love⟫, to feel and exhibit esteem and goodwill to a person, to prize and delight in a thing.
⟪1.⟫ Of human affection, to men: τ. πλησίον, ⟦Matthew 5:43|Mt 5:43⟧; τ. ἐχθρούς, ⟦Matthew 5:44|ib. 44⟧; to Christ, ⟦John 8:42|Jo 8:42⟧; to God, ⟦Matthew 22:37|Mt 22:37⟧; c. acc. rei, ⟦Luke 11:43|Lk 11:43⟧, ⟦John 12:43|Jo 12:43⟧, ⟦Ephesians 5:25|Eph 5:25⟧, ⟦2 Timothy 4:8|II Tim 4:8⟧, ⟦2 Timothy 4:10|10⟧, ⟦Hebrews 1:9|He 1:9⟧, ⟦1 Peter 2:17|I Pe 2:17⟧, ⟦1 Peter 3:10|3:10⟧, ⟦2 Peter 2:15|II Pe 2:15⟧, ⟦1 John 2:15|I Jo 2:15⟧, ⟦Revelation 12:11|Re 12:11⟧.
⟪2.⟫ Of divine love;
	⟪(a)⟫ God's love: to men, ⟦Romans 8:37|Ro 8:37⟧; to Christ, ⟦John 3:35|Jo 3:35⟧;
	⟪(b)⟫ Christ's love: to men, ⟦Mark 10:21|Mk 10:21⟧; to God, ⟦John 14:31|Jo 14:31⟧; c. cogn. acc., ⟦John 17:26|Jo 17:26⟧, ⟦Ephesians 2:4|Eph 2:4⟧.
SYN.: φιλέω. From its supposed etymology (Thayer, LS; but v. also Boisacq) ἀ. is commonly understood properly to denote love based on esteem (diligo), as distinct from that expressed by φιλέω (amo), spontaneous natural affection, emotional and unreasoning. If this distinction holds, ἀ. is fitly used in NT of Christian love to God and man, the spiritual affection which follows the direction of the will, and which, therefore, unlike that feeling which is instinctive and unreasoned, can be commanded as a duty. (Cf. ἀγάπη, and v. Tr., Syn. §xii; Cremer, 9, 592; and esp. MM, VGT, s.v.)

	⟪(a)⟫ of things and places which have a claim to reverence as sacred to God, e.g. the Temple: ⟦Matthew 24:15|Mt 24:15⟧, ⟦Hebrews 9:1|He 9:1⟧;

	⟪(a)⟫ of Christ, ⟦Mark 1:24|Mk 1:24⟧, ⟦John 6:69|Jo 6:69⟧, ⟦Acts 4:30|Ac 4:30⟧;
	⟪(b)⟫ of Christians, ⟦Acts 9:13|Ac 9:13⟧, ⟦Romans 1:7|Ro 1:7⟧, ⟦Hebrews 6:10|He 6:10⟧, ⟦Revelation 5:8|Re 5:8⟧.
⟪3.⟫ In the moral sense of sharing God's purity: ⟦Mark 6:20|Mk 6:20⟧, ⟦John 17:11|Jo 17:11⟧, ⟦Acts 3:14|Ac 3:14⟧, ⟦Revelation 3:7|Re 3:7⟧.
⟪4.⟫ Of pure, clean sacrifices and offerings: ⟦1 Corinthians 7:14|I Co 7:14⟧, ⟦Ephesians 1:4|Eph 1:4⟧.
SYN.: ἁγνός, pure, both in ceremonial and spiritual sense; ἱερός (sacer), sacred, that which is inviolable because of its (external) relation to God; ὅσιος (sanctus as opp. to nefas), that which is based on everlasting ordinances of right. G80.b:
⟪ἀδελφός⟫, -οῦ, ὁ
(< ἀ- copul., δελφύς, womb), in cl., ⟪a brother⟫, born of the same parent or parents. [In LXX (Hort, Ja., 102 f.), for ⁨אָח⁩;]
⟪1.⟫ lit. of a brother (⟦Genesis 4:2|Ge 4:2⟧, al.).
⟪2.⟫ Of a neighbour (⟦Leviticus 19:17|Le 19:17⟧).
⟪3.⟫ Of a member of the same nation (⟦Exodus 2:14|Ex 2:14⟧, ⟦Deuteronomy 15:3|De 15:3⟧). In NT in each of these senses (1. ⟦Matthew 1:2|Mt 1:2⟧, al.; 2. ⟦Matthew 7:3|Mt 7:3⟧; 3. ⟦Romans 9:3|Ro 9:3⟧) and also,
⟪4.⟫ of a fellow-Christian: ⟦1 Corinthians 1:1|I Co 1:1⟧, ⟦Acts 9:30|Ac 9:30⟧. This usage finds illustration in π., where ἀ. is used of members of a pagan religious community (M, Th., I, 1:4; MM, VGT, s.v.). The ἀδελφοὶ τ. Κυρίου (⟦Matthew 12:46|Mt 12:46-49⟧ ⟦Matthew 13:55|13:55⟧ ⟦Matthew 28:10|28:10⟧, ⟦Mark 3:31|Mk 3:31-34⟧, ⟦Luke 8:19|Lk 8:19-21⟧, ⟦John 2:12|Jo 2:12⟧ ⟦John 7:3|7:3⟧, ⟦John 7:5|5⟧ ⟦John 7:10|10⟧ ⟦John 20:17|20:17⟧, ⟦Acts 1:14|Ac 1:14⟧, ⟦1 Corinthians 9:5|I Co 9:5⟧) may have been sons of Joseph and Mary (Mayor, Ja., Intr. viff.; DB, i, 320 ff.) or of Joseph by a former marriage (Lft., Gal., 252ff.; DCG, i, 232 ff.), but the view of Jerome, which makes ἀ. equivalent to ἀνεψιός, is inconsistent with Greek usage. (Cremer, 66.)
